analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlooks Survey recorded 21.2% of utilities firms using AI in the most recent period, up from 12.6% in the prior period, a gain that positions the sector meaningfully above many service industries even before oil and gas extraction, which the Census Bureau reports under mining rather than utilities, is counted. The jump suggests adoption is accelerating rather than plateauing, though the figure covers only the utilities NAICS code and does not capture the full breadth of AI activity across the energy complex.

The uses of AI in energy span two quite different parts of the industry. On the grid and renewables side, the Department of Energy's AI office covers applications in real-time grid balancing, reactor optimization, and carbon capture, while DOE's Grid Modernization Initiative funds AI projects across US utilities through the Grid Modernization Laboratory Consortium, a strategic partnership with the national laboratories. NextEra Energy, described as the largest US renewable producer, applies AI to wind and solar yield forecasting, battery dispatch optimization, and automated plant maintenance. Amperon, founded in 2018, sells AI and machine learning driven load, price, and renewable forecasts to utilities and traders, claiming accuracy up to three times better than legacy forecasting solutions by analyzing roughly 25 weather variables every hour across 40,000 granular weather points drawn from four vendors and blending outputs from three of them through an ensemble model.

In the upstream oil and gas world, Baker Hughes describes its portfolio as enriched by digitalization, artificial intelligence, and automation capabilities that enable remote operations, reduce risk, and drive decarbonization, with industrial solutions that surface insights across asset, process, and sustainability performance to support data-driven decisions. Geoteric applies deep learning and computer vision directly to three-dimensional seismic data, offering tools through its AI Hub that allow geoscientists to compare AI networks and scenarios for mapping subsurface faults and geological features, with the company describing the technology as revolutionizing upstream exploration efforts and helping to digitize and decarbonize operations globally. Siemens Energy positions itself as a supplier of AI controllers and digital-twin software for gas, wind, and grid assets, meaning that for many operators AI arrives embedded in equipment rather than as a separately procured software layer.

The standards and research infrastructure underpinning these deployments is substantial. IEEE's Power and Energy Society produces over 900 standards through its technical committee working groups, covering machine learning in power systems, grid cyber-defense, and distributed energy resource management, and publishes leading technical journals on the subject. The Electric Power Research Institute serves as the sector's shared research layer, running working groups on AI grid resilience, wildfire-risk prediction, and asset-health monitoring. This combination of federal programs, industry consortia, and standards bodies gives the energy sector a more organized technical governance layer than many industries of comparable size.

Energy occupies an unusual dual position in the AI economy: it is both a user of AI and the binding constraint on AI's expansion. Per the Department of Energy, data centers consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and are projected to reach between 6.7 and 12% by 2028, with AI identified as the primary driver of that growth. DOE has announced plans to partner with private-sector developers to build AI data centers and energy generation projects on DOE lands, and launched the Speed to Power Initiative to accelerate large-scale grid infrastructure development. DOE acknowledges the risks directly, noting that AI systems may generate incorrect, unverifiable, and potentially harmful outputs and that any use must properly understand and mitigate those risks, a posture that reflects the safety-critical nature of grid infrastructure rather than a general reluctance toward the technology.

For an operator considering deployment, the sector picture suggests that AI in energy is not experimental at the leading edge: large utilities and oilfield services companies are running production systems for forecasting, maintenance, and subsurface analysis, specialist vendors with track records exist at multiple price points, and federal programs provide both funding pathways and technical guidance. The more practical constraints are data quality, the integration complexity of legacy grid infrastructure, and the cybersecurity exposure that IEEE PES standards work is designed to address. The Census adoption figure also implies that roughly four in five utilities firms have not yet answered yes to using AI in the prior two weeks, leaving substantial room for the adoption curve to continue rising.
